title: Pixellab?
author: Suitable_Sport4709
selftext:
So this is a bit of a vent. Ive been working to try to get a reasonable pipeline to do pixel art using AI in my game. So far Ive settled on blender, aseprite, and pixellab which are all attached to claude via mcp.

Pixellab has a website that provides a UI for image generation. Holy crap is it an AI fever dream. The UI is incoherent and clicking banners buttons sends you all over the place to quasi-defunct site pages. Pretty nuts that this slop seems to be best the best on the market.

The actual pixellab images at first look pretty good but controlling asset size and character size is a mess. For example, I want a 35px chibi character but it will only produce 27px characters. For larger characters like 50px the variance between animations is noticeable at +/- 4 px.

At this point, Im close to just giving up. Ive tried a chatgpt image pipeline which couldn't get the job done. Blender + meshy + aseprite couldn't get the job done. Pixellab cant seem to do it. Is it just not possible to create coherent art assets with ai? Am I the problem here or are the tools just far from ready and too immature at this stage?

For reference, I was trying to make a top down pixel art rpg that has elements of an elden ring/skyrim-type adventure.

comments.author: keytonw
comments.body: I had exactly the same reaction to the UI. I have since stopped using the UI and have handled Claude Code an api key and life has become much better since. You might try that approach. It works much better than expected.

replies.body:
Yes this seems like the answer + the aseprite plugin... but come on! The dev should be ashamed of their blatant ai slop website. Like have some pride in your work man!

Have you managed to create a pipeline of consistent assets?

replies.author: StarMonkeyGames
replies.body:
Thanks for the tip. My god the UI and limitations. But hey, they put a full editor in it. I feel like this isn't some corporate company, it's just a small dev team during their best. And sometimes opportunity costs justify not updating the website.

Besides that. Like you said, I use pixellabs and another model together. They compensate each other and I get quality sprite sheets out.

And let's be fair. Rapid art, music, and code development for is now available for like $30 bucks a month.

I'll take it.

comments.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
comments.body:
I use the pixellab aseprite plugin which I like better. The ui is still kind of bad but overall I really like pixel lab.

You could do a mix of handcraft and gen if you felt comfortable with that. Character like make a very basic or even bad 36px character… then go to edit image and prompt something like “make character look more chibi and better. lol sometimes I draw my own asset, am not happy with it and just prompt “make better” and I get results I like.

comments.author: ThePhallusofGod
comments.body:
I don't know exactly the art you're wanting for your game - but if I were you I'd be making my own tools.

Draw a rough sketch yourself, spend a little time drawing one good median sized character - even a bit bad, you can tweak it later.
Use layers. Define the shapes of heads, bodies, hands, whatever.
You tell your agent that these are the blueprints. You tell it these are the median sizes for my characters. You set bounds for now much it's allowed outside those medians.
You draw shading - and ask it to make gradients that fit the style you present. You can use 3d for this under the hood if you want, but present it on a pixel grid. 3d lighting is easier obviously.
Generate algorithms as you go for exactly the style you're after, dithering, outlines, whatever you like.
If you have good constraints (eyes are never more than X pixels apart, for example) and have a style idea in mind - AI will generate you usable art. AI image generation in my opinion sucks for making game assets because they're not made of layers and pieces according to a schema.

As soon as you define your schema and generate them with code and procedures, you'll be having a better time.
